newsitem.title: UK: Mitsubishi seeks Jan 20-25 tanker from Iraqi Bakr-.
newsitem.headline: Mitsubishi seeks Jan 20-25 tanker from Iraqi Bakr-.

text.p: Japanese company Mitsubishi Corp has asked tanker brokers about the availability of ships to load Iraqi crude oil from the Middle East Gulf terminal of Mina al-Bakr on January 20-25, trading sources said.
The sources said Mitsubishi had not yet signed a supply contract with Iraqi state oil marketer SOMO but was anticipating doing so soon and sought the vessel now.
Mitsubishi is due to act as an agent for about five Japanese oil companies to buy Iraqi oil under a limited oil sale plan that got the go-ahead from the United Nations on Monday.
The Japanese firm sent a representative last week to Baghdad.
A spokeswoman for Mitsubishi declined to comment on the tanker enquiries.
"For the moment, we would like to refrain from confirming or denying questions related to the issue of Iraqi oil," the spokeswoman said.
Questions about the fitness of the war-damaged Mina al-Bakr leads many shipping sources to believe that no exports from there will be possible before the end of the year.
Sources close to Dutch-based Saybolt, the United Nations-appointed inspectors, said the lines and equipment at the terminal "are not totally acceptable."
"Some of the pipelines have rusted and corroded and need to be replaced," a source close to Saybolt said.

Mina al-Bakr is Iraq's main export point for crude oil shipments to Asia but the bulk of its exports would be channelled through Turkey's Ceyhan which is linked by pipeline to Iraqi oil centre, Kirkuk.
Iraq began on Tuesday pumping 650,000 barrels of crude oil through its pipeline to Turkey.
Iraq also said oil from the Mina al-Bakr terminal would start to flow on Friday or Saturday. But shipping sources said it would take at least one week to test the metering equipment at the terminal.
"At the earliest, oil will flow from al-Bakr in 10 days," a shipping source said.

Shipping sources said that though there remained concerns about debris and mines around the offshore loading terminal, there would probably be a number of tanker owners willing to take their vessels there.
"Owners of old ships will take their ships about anywhere. But whether oil companies will charter the rust buckets is another matter," one ship broker said.

One shipping source suggested that Japanese oil companies, which typically will only charter modern, high-quality vessels, may charter older ships to load from Mina al-Bakr and then transfer into more modern vessels at Fujairah.
